content.summary_of_the_paper: This work proposes a training method to fine-tune language models (LMs) by combining adversarial training and gradient masking. During the fine-tuning stage, some artificially constructed noises are added into the clean samples to craft adversarial examples, and the crafted examples are merged with the clean ones to train the task-specific models. In addition, some gradients will be randomly masked and not used to update the parameters of the models (the probabilities of the gradients being masked are proportional to the squares of their magnitudes). The experimental results on two text classification datasets show that the proposed method slightly improve the robustness of fined-tuned models, compared to the selected baselines.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

(1) The idea of masking gradients seems to be new, and it is worthwhile to investigate how to improve the robustness of NLP models in various aspects (including distribution-shift generalization, adversarial robustness, calibrated prediction, and anomaly detection) by a training method.

(2) The experimental results on two datasets show that the proposed fine-tuning method can slightly improve the text classification models in their distribution-shift generalization, adversarial robustness, calibrated prediction, and anomaly detection.

Weaknesses:

(1) It is unclear why the proposed masking gradients can improve the robustness of NLP models in theory. The gradient masking only can help to prevent the fine-tuned models from deviating too much from a pre-trained language model (LM). It seems that the gradient-masking strategy cannot improve the robustness of the resulting models. Besides, large language models were also proven to be vulnerable to adversarial perturbations.

(2) As shown in Tables 1 and 2, the improvement of the fine-tuned models trained with the proposed method is not significant (less than 0.5%), compared to the selected baselines. Besides, some strong training methods were not compared, such as FreeLB [1] and FreeLB++ [2].

[1] Zhu et al. FreeLB: Enhanced adversarial training for natural language understanding. ICLR, 2020.

[2] Li et al. Searching for an Effective Defender: Benchmarking Defense against Adversarial Word Substitution. EMNLP, 2021.

(3) Only two datasets (i.e., SST-2 and MNLI) were used to evaluate the proposed method. It seems that the proposed training method also can be applied to the computer vision (CV) models. It would be better to report the results on CV tasks.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is well organized and written in general. It is somewhat novel to improve the robustness of models on the fine-tuning stage by masking gradients. However, it is unclear why the proposed masking gradients can improve the robustness of NLP models in theory.
content.summary_of_the_review: This work proposes to improve the robustness of models in various aspects by combining adversarial training and gradient masking. However, the authors fail to explain well why the gradient masking performed during the fine-tuning stage contributes to the improvement of the resulting model’s robustness. The improvement of the fine-tuned models trained with the proposed method is not significant, and some strong baselines were not compared. Besides, only two text classification datasets were used to evaluate the proposed method.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes an adversarial finetuning framework to improve the robustness of fine-tuned pretrained language models. Specifically, it adopts the adversarial training framework and randomly masks some gradients during optimization for dealing with the forgetting problem. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in terms of robust accuracy, calibration, and anomaly detection.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength

1. Overall the paper is well-written and the method is clearly presented.

2. Though the adversarial fine-tuning part is from previous work, the proposed gradient masking technique looks novel to me.

Weaknesses

1. [1] proposes an adversarial fine-tuning method that addresses the forgetting problem from an information theoretical perspective. [2] proposes to randomly preserve some initial parameters during fine-tuning. Both of them are very related and should be compared or at least discussed.

2. The motivation for the use of gradient masking is not very clear to me. Admittedly gradient masking can prevent the parameters from deviating too much from the pre-trained parameters. However, the change in the parameter space has a very complicated relationship to the change in the parameter space. In this sense, why gradient masking can differentiate which parameters correspond to the generalizable knowledge and preserve the generalizable knowledge only?  It would help if the authors can make this story more solid.

[1] Xinshuai Dong, Luu Anh Tuan, Min Lin, Shuicheng Yan, Hanwang Zhang. "How Should Pre-Trained Language Models Be Fine-Tuned Towards Adversarial Robustness?." In NeurIPS 2021.

[2] Cheolhyoung Lee, Kyunghyun Cho, and Wanmo Kang. Mixout: Effective regularization to finetune large-scale pretrained language models. In ICLR, 2020.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Overall the writing is good and the gradient masking part is novel to me.

content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, the robustness of fine-tuned LMs is considered in terms of distribution-shift generalization, adversarial robustness, model calibration, and anomaly detection. To improve this robustness, a method combining gradient importance sampling and adversarial training is proposed in this paper. However, practical applications regarding this setting should be clarified. The experimental results are not sufficient to prove the effectiveness of the method.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1) In this paper, a new benchmark is proposed to evaluate the robustness of fine-tuned LM in terms of four representative aspects of model robustness.
2) The authors have conducted a large number of experiments in an attempt to verify the effectiveness of the proposed method.
3) This paper is well-written and easy to understand.

Weaknesses:
1) The proposed approach is based on adversarial training in a finite parameter space, which may not match my intuition as to why it can improve the performance of model calibration and anomaly detection. It needs more analysis.
2) As I understand, the purpose of LP-FT is to improve model dispersion, so why does LP-FT improve the performance of adversarial robustness, model calibration, and anomaly detection?
3) Some important and competitive baselines are missing: RIFT [1] (designed to improve adversarial robustness while avoiding catastrophic forgetting) and InfoBERT [2] (designed to improve the robustness of language models in standard and adversarial training).
4) As can be seen in Table 10, the AdvWeight (Adversarial Training) does not work well, which is inconsistent with the findings in the previous paper [3] and even weaker than LP-FT (a method that does not consider adversarial robustness). Therefore, I suspect that the AdvWeight was not properly tuned and the authors need to provide the number of perturbation steps (not just the perturbation size) used in the AdvWeight.
5) Why does only updating the selective model parameters perform better than AdvEmbed in the ablation study? And does AdvEmbed in Table 4 use the bidirectional KL divergence in Eq. (1)?
6) Adversarial training in a finite weight parameter space is one of the innovative points of this paper, and the authors need to compare it with other finite space optimization methods to highlight the effectiveness of important weight parameters sampling, for example, adversarial training on some layers, combine adversarial training with Child-tuning and Subspace AT [4].
7) The authors need to provide sensitivity tests of the proposed method to hyper-parameters, such as masking ratio, smoothness factor, and coefficient for consistency regularization.

[1] RIFT, Dong, X., Luu, A., Lin, M., Yan, S., & Zhang, H. (2021). How Should Pre-Trained Language Models Be Fine-Tuned Towards Adversarial Robustness? NeurIPS, 2021.
[2] InfoBERT, Wang, Boxin et al. InfoBERT: Improving Robustness of Language Models from An Information Theoretic Perspective. ICLR 2021.
[3] Li, Zongyi et al. Searching for an Effective Defender: Benchmarking Defense against Adversarial Word Substitution. EMNLP 2021.
[4] Subspace AT. Li, T., Wu, Y., Chen, S., Fang, K., & Huang, X. (2022). Subspace Adversarial Training. 2022 IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR), 13399-13408.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
1)	Authors need to provide the purpose of baselines in the A.2 are designed, and the benefits that can be gained, to help readers better understand them.
2)	The authors need to provide some real-world scenarios to help the reader understand why it is necessary to consider four robustness metrics at the same time.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper suggests two training strategies to improve the robustness of a language model. The first approach is using an adversarial training, and the second approach is zeroing out some of the gradients during training. The proposed approach is tested with 2 datasets and 5 evaluation metrics. The proposed approach shows the best overall performance among 13 methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
- S1: The proposed approach shows the overall best performance among 13 methods. 
- S2: The approach is simple and can be easily adoptable to other domains.
- S3: Base model, ablation study, and qualitative analysis are performed.

Weaknesses
- W1: The proposed approach is a loose combination of existing approaches, and the comparison to those is not discussed.
- W2: Adversarial robustness evaluation was only done in a transfer attack fashion with a pre-generated adversarial test dataset.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is mostly clearly written, and the evaluation is mostly thoroughly done. Some details had to be put in the appendix. I believe the text is original, but the approaches themselves are known. There are minor typos such as 'peturbation'.
content.summary_of_the_review:
This paper empirically shows the improved robustness of a combination of known approaches. The proposed approach seems to belong to a category of "Dropout regularizations that inject noise into intermediate activations when training deep neural networks" as described in the related work section of "Regularizing Meta-Learning via Gradient Dropout," Tseng et al, 2020. While the paper is well written, it doesn't discuss in detail how the proposed approach is different from selective reflection of gradients or dropout, as well as common adversarial training. Also, the proposed combination of 4 components don't seem to be rather independent except for the use of Bernoulli distribution, and thus this combination process doesn't provide technical contribution. And how each or the combination makes the multiple aspects simultaneously better. While the quality of writing itself and the empirical result is encouraging, I want these to be clarified before getting this published.

Again, mainly two questions to be addressed:
- Q1. How are these approaches different from existing ones?
- Q2. Why these 4 components?
- Q3. How do they improve multiple aspects of robustness?

content.title: Robustifying Language Models via Adversarial Training with Masked Gradient
content.abstract: Fine-tuning pre-trained language models (LMs) has become the de-facto standard method for improving state-of-the-art performances on various NLP tasks. Although these models are usually evaluated with accuracy on fixed validation sets, it is insufficient for the reliable deployment of fine-tuned LMs in real-world settings, as there are known issues within existing model evaluations, such as adversarial robustness and model calibration. To address such issues, we propose a simple yet effective training algorithm, coined Robustifying LMs via Adversarial training with Masked gradient (RAM), to improve the robustness of fine-tuned LMs. In particular, we leverage adversarial training to robustify LMs for various types of perturbations. Simultaneously, to prevent the trained model from largely deviating from the initial pre-trained model, we selectively update the important model parameters using the masked gradients; their relative importance is obtained from the gradients calculated during training. Consequently, it enables the model to preserve the generalizability of the pre-trained model while improving its robustness. Additionally, we construct a new benchmark to evaluate the robustness of fine-tuned LMs in terms of four representative aspects of model robustness in a unified way. Under these benchmarks, we demonstrate the effectiveness of RAM compared to other state-of-the-art fine-tuning methods, and verify that RAM is successfully robustifying various types of LMs. Our work suggests a rethinking of the robustness aspect of LMs as an essential direction for their reliable deployment, along with a simple yet effective solution.
